download.title: Download LivePlay
download.subtitle: Free and open-source. Available for Windows, macOS, and Linux.

macGatekeeper.title: macOS: "LivePlay is damaged and can't be opened"?
macGatekeeper.intro: LivePlay is not yet signed with an Apple Developer certificate, so macOS quarantines it on download. The app is safe — this just means Apple hasn't been paid to notarize it. To open it, remove the quarantine flag once after installing to /Applications:
macGatekeeper.outro: Enter your password when prompted, then launch LivePlay normally. You only need to do this once per install.

winSmartScreen.title: Windows: "Windows protected your PC"?
winSmartScreen.intro: LivePlay isn't yet signed with a certificate Microsoft SmartScreen recognises, so Windows may show a blue "Windows protected your PC" warning when you run the installer. The app is safe — it simply hasn't built up download reputation yet (code signing is on the way).
winSmartScreen.step1: Click "More info" on the warning dialog.
winSmartScreen.step2: Click the "Run anyway" button that appears, then continue the installation normally.
winSmartScreen.outro: If your browser blocked the download instead, choose "Keep" to save the installer first.

contribute.title: Contribute
contribute.subtitle: LivePlay is free and open-source — and always will be.
contribute.freeText: LivePlay is completely free to download and use — no licence fees, no subscriptions, no paywalls. Every feature is available to everyone, with no premium tiers.
contribute.licenseText: LivePlay is released under the GNU AGPL-3.0 licence. In plain terms: you are free to use, study, share and modify it. If you share a modified version — or run it as a network service — you must make your source code available under the same licence, so the whole community keeps benefiting.
contribute.contributeText: Anyone can contribute. Report bugs, suggest features, improve translations or submit code — every contribution is welcome. Head to the GitHub repository to open an issue or a pull request.

interface.title: Intuitive Interface
interface.description: LivePlay features a clean, simple and modern interface designed specifically for live sound operators. Organize your main sound files in playlists, and add sounds to a cart player for quick access or announcements. Audio files added to the cart will automatically behave as announcements, ducking any background audio when played.

audioEngine.title: Robust C++ Audio Engine
audioEngine.description: At the heart of LivePlay is a dedicated, high-performance audio engine written in C++ that talks directly to your sound hardware — WASAPI on Windows, Core Audio on macOS, and ALSA on Linux. Every cue runs as a fully independent playback instance with its own decoder and fade envelope, so playing the same file twice at different volumes always behaves exactly as expected. The engine runs as a standalone server process: it can live inside the desktop app, or run headless on a dedicated backstage machine wired to your audio interfaces.

limiter.title: Brick-Wall Limiter & Loudness Targets
limiter.description: A true brick-wall limiter sits on every output channel, keeping your levels consistent and protecting your hardware and audience from runaway peaks. Choose from built-in output targets that match professional loudness standards — EBU R128, streaming, radio, Netflix and live — and LivePlay applies the right ceiling, metering zones and waveform calibration automatically.

meters.title: Broadcast-Grade Metering
meters.description: Trust what you hear with real-time, broadcast-quality metering at every stage of the signal path — per-cue, per mixer channel, and on the master output. Colour-coded meter zones follow the loudness target you've selected, so you can see at a glance whether you're sitting comfortably within spec or pushing into the red.

routing.title: Multi-Device Audio Routing
routing.description: Every cue plays through a mixer bus, and every bus sends to a hardware output, to another bus, or to the Preview bus for headphones — across multiple sound cards at once. The Master bus is the house: it sends to "Main Out", which is your default sound card until you map it to something else. Pick a device or output straight from a strip, or open "Remap hardware outputs" in the mixer header to bind logical outputs like FOH or Foyer to real channels — so a show travels between venues without being rewired.

previewLtc.title: Dedicated Preview & LTC Timecode
previewLtc.description: Audition cues silently through the mixer's Preview bus — the strip PFL and the headphone preview button both land on — without ever touching your main outputs, so you can line up the next cue while the show rolls on. Give the Preview bus a device or output on its strip and it is ready; its fader is your headphone level. A separate SMPTE LTC timecode generator outputs a continuous linear timecode signal on its own channel, letting you synchronise lighting desks, video playback and other external devices to LivePlay.

waveform.title: Waveform Trimmer
waveform.description: Trim your audio with precision using the built-in waveform editor. Set in and out points, adjust volume, and configure fade times visually. You can also automatically trim based on silence, or automatically adjust the volume so that all audio levels are consistent.

youtube.title: YouTube Integration
youtube.description: Download audio directly from YouTube with our built-in downloader! Perfect for quickly adding music, sound effects, or backing tracks to your show (please make sure you have the rights to use the content or are using public domain content).

properties.title: Easy to use Properties Panel
properties.description: Change the name, color, and playback properties of your audio files with ease. Set files to loop, adjust their volume, start and end behaviours, and configure automatic silence trimming all from one convenient location. You are in control of your show's flow!

ducking.title: Automatic Ducking
ducking.description: Configure automatic ducking to lower the volume of background music when announcements or dialogue play. Perfect for smooth transitions in live productions.

discovery.title: Automatic Discovery & Rock-Solid Reliability
discovery.description: LivePlay servers announce themselves on your local network, so clients find them automatically — no IP addresses to type in. If the audio engine ever stops unexpectedly, it relaunches itself instantly and resumes playback right where it left off, so your show keeps running. And because the engine is a true server, multiple clients can connect to the same instance at once — ideal for a primary operator and a backup, or a stage manager monitoring playback alongside the sound op.

remoteOperation.title: Local or Remote Operation
remoteOperation.description: The LivePlay audio server launches automatically alongside the application, or can be run on a dedicated backstage machine with your audio interfaces plugged in. Connect from any computer on the same network and take full control — transport, properties, routing, and live metering all work remotely, giving you the flexibility to separate your control position from your audio hardware.

firstLaunch.title: Quick Setup
firstLaunch.description: Get started in seconds with LivePlay's streamlined setup process. Select a folder, create a project and start importing files! All your media gets automatically collected into one place so you can move your project between computers with ease.

ports.title: Network Ports
ports.subtitle: If you're running the server and client on different machines, make sure these ports are open on your network and firewall.

control.title: Control Surface
control.description: REST API and WebSocket connection carrying transport commands, project data, routing and live meters between the client and server.

discovery.title: Automatic Discovery
discovery.description: Broadcast and multicast beacon (group 239.255.69.80) that lets clients find LivePlay servers on the local network automatically.

ports.note: A single-machine install needs no configuration — the client and server talk over 127.0.0.1 and the Windows installer adds the firewall rules for you. These ports only matter when separating the control position from the audio hardware across a LAN.

settings.title: Where settings live
settings.subtitle: LivePlay keeps configuration in four places. Which one a value lives in decides whether it travels with your show, follows the person, or stays on the machine.

server.name: Server
server.owns: How the engine runs and binds, the venue’s named outputs, and the accounts
server.travels: No — it belongs to the rack

user.name: User
user.owns: Language, theme, meter unit and transport keys
user.travels: No — it follows the person to any machine they sign in on

project.name: Project
project.owns: The show: cues, buses, routing, fades and everything the audience hears
project.travels: Yes — this is the show file

machine.name: Machine
machine.owns: Window and pane layout, Show Mode, and which server this install talks to
machine.travels: No — and nothing about the show may depend on it

settings.note: A value that changes what the audience hears is never stored outside the show file. That one rule is why a show sounds the same in another building.

api.title: External control / API
api.subtitle: Drive LivePlay from lighting consoles, Stream Deck, Companion, or your own scripts.

intro.title: The basics
intro.description: Every LivePlay server answers plain HTTP on TCP port 4480 — the same interface the LivePlay app itself uses — so anything that can send a web request can run a show. Requests and replies are JSON. Replace <server> below with the server's IP address or host name (127.0.0.1 on the machine running LivePlay).
intro.getVsPost: Anything that accepts GET can be fired by simply opening the URL — from a browser, a Stream Deck "Open URL" button or a lighting console's HTTP action. Calls that are POST only must be sent as a POST request: opening them in a browser sends a GET, and the server refuses it.
intro.stopWarning: That is why changing "play" to "stop" in the API Trigger URL from the Properties panel doesn't work in a browser: …/play accepts GET, but …/stop, …/pause, …/resume and …/seek are POST only. Send them with curl, Companion, or any tool that can make a POST request.

controls.title: Common controls
controls.description: The calls show-control users reach for most. <uuid> is an item's id: it is part of the API Trigger URL in the Properties panel, and GET /api/project/items lists every item's uuid.

go.description: GO — play whatever is armed as Up Next, exactly like the GO button in the app.

stopAll.notes: Optional body {"fade_ms": n}. Without it the project's Stop All fade is used (1000 ms unless changed); 0 = cut. Also stops the preview audition unless the project is set not to.

playItem.description: Play one item — an audio item, or a group (which starts according to its start behaviour).
playItem.notes: This is the API Trigger URL from the Properties panel. Honours the item's in-point, fades, ducking and end behaviour. Works with a group's uuid too.

playIndex.description: Play an item by its position in the playlist — audio item or group.
playIndex.notes: The path is zero-based and descends into groups: 0 = the first item, 5 = the sixth, 1,2 = the third item inside the second top-level item (a group); 1/2 works too. It stays zero-based even if the app is set to number cues from 1.

stopItem.description: Stop one item. For a group, stops whatever is playing inside it.
stopItem.notes: POST only. Fades over the item's Stop fade; optional body {"fade_ms": n} overrides it for this stop, 0 = cut.

pauseItem.description: Pause one item, holding its playhead.

resumeItem.description: Resume a paused item from where it was paused.

playSelected.description: Play the item selected in the playlist (the app's Enter key).

pauseToggle.description: Pause everything on air — or, if anything is paused, resume it.
pauseToggle.notes: One button that is never ambiguous about which way it will go.

armSelected.description: Set the selected item as Up Next, so the next GO plays it.
armSelected.notes: Same as "Set As Next" in the app.

cart.notes: Zero-based: cart button 1 is /cart/0/play, button 2 is /cart/1/play. Returns 404 if the slot is empty.

masterGain.description: Read or set the engine-wide output trim, in dB.
masterGain.notes: GET reads it. POST {"db": -6} sets it; {"delta": -1} nudges it. This is not the Master bus fader — that is PATCH /api/buses/<id> {"gainDb": …} on the bus whose master flag is true.

stateSummary.description: One compact snapshot of the show.
stateSummary.notes: What is playing (with elapsed and remaining time), what is Up Next, the selection, cart slots, buses, the master trim and Show Mode. Fetch it once on connect, then follow the WebSocket instead of polling.

listItems.description: List the playlist items with their uuid, name and type.
listItems.notes: Top-level items, paged with ?offset=0&limit=100; groups carry their children inline.

examples.title: Try it with curl
examples.description: GO, stop one item with a 3-second fade, then stop everything:
examples.curl:
curl http://<server>:4480/api/transport/go

curl -X POST http://<server>:4480/api/project/items/<uuid>/stop \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"fade_ms": 3000}'

curl -X POST http://<server>:4480/api/transport/stop_all

more.title: Beyond the basics
more.description: A few more calls controllers commonly use:

selection.description: read the shared playlist selection, or move it: {"delta": 1} steps down, {"delta": -1} steps up, {"itemUuid": "…"} selects one item.

buses.description: list the mixer buses and change one — for example {"gainDb": -3} or {"mute": true}.

limiter.description: read or switch the master limiter; a POST without "enabled" toggles it.

showMode.description: read or switch Show Mode; a POST without "enabled" toggles it.

auth.title: Logins and browser remotes
auth.description: Out of the box a LivePlay server asks for no login. Once an administrator creates user accounts, every request must carry a token in an "Authorization: Bearer <token>" header. Get one by logging in — tokens last 30 days:
auth.login:
curl -X POST http://<server>:4480/api/auth/login \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"name": "sam", "password": "…"}'
# → { "token": "lp1.…", "expiresIn": 2592000, "user": { … } }

curl -H "Authorization: Bearer lp1.…" http://<server>:4480/api/transport/go
auth.headerNote: The token is only accepted in that header, never in the URL, so a plain "open URL" button cannot trigger a server that has accounts — use a tool that can send headers. The WebSocket is the one exception: connect to /ws?access_token=<token>.
auth.cors: Browser-based remotes (a web page calling the API with fetch) work: the server answers CORS preflight requests and accepts any origin by default. To allow only your own remote, start the server with --cors-origin https://your-remote.example — this also restricts which web pages may open the WebSocket.

websocket.title: The WebSocket
websocket.description: For two-way control without polling, connect to ws://<server>:4480/ws. Every frame is a JSON object with a "type". Frames you can send:
websocket.framesNote: play with a group's uuid starts the group according to its start behaviour. Leave out fade_ms to use the item's own Stop fade (or, for stop_all, the project's Stop All fade).
websocket.pushTitle: The server pushes, without being asked:

snapshot.name: playback_snapshot
snapshot.description: once, right after you connect: every cue on air and what is Up Next.

cueState.name: cue_state
cueState.description: on every transport change of a cue — playing, fading out, paused or stopped.

meters.name: meters
meters.description: a continuous stream of per-cue, per-bus and per-output levels for metering (30 times a second by default).

docPatch.name: doc_patch
docPatch.description: on every change to the show — items, buses, selection, Up Next, Show Mode and more — so your copy of the state never drifts.

companion.title: Bitfocus Companion
companion.description: A community-built Companion module drives LivePlay from Stream Deck and every other surface Companion supports. It isn't in the official Companion module store yet, so it has to be sideloaded — follow the instructions in its repository:

discovery.title: Finding a server
discovery.description: The server periodically broadcasts (and multicasts) a JSON beacon on UDP 4481, and answers a unicast solicitation immediately. The payload:
discovery.note: Send {"type":"liveplay-solicit"} to UDP 4481 to provoke an immediate unicast reply instead of waiting for the next periodic broadcast.
